name: polling-consumer
intent: Let the application decide when it receives a message: the consumer explicitly pulls a bounded batch from the channel instead of the transport pushing messages into it, so the pull rate, idle behaviour and acknowledgement point stay under the consumer's control.
problem: The channel cannot push - or must not. Either the transport only answers requests (a broker consumer API, a database table used as a queue, a filesystem drop, a request-based device), or the consumer must not be handed more work than it can process, so push delivery would force it to accept an unbounded stream it cannot flow-control.
context: Messaging endpoints at the edge of an application, in front of a channel whose delivery is pull-based or whose rate must be throttled; typically a thread, task or coroutine that owns a receive loop, an acknowledgement mechanism (offset, receipt handle, queue removal) and a shutdown path. Brokered consumers (Kafka-style fetch protocols), batch/ETL drains and downstream-limited workers are the canonical settings.
benefits: The consumer controls the rate: backpressure is inherent - it simply does not pull while it has no capacity.
Works where push is unavailable or undesirable: broker pull protocols, database tables, request-only legacy devices, and upstream APIs that would be hammered by a subscription.
Messages arrive as ordinary call results in the consumer's own thread or task, so processing needs no callback discipline and business logic stays free of transport callbacks.
Batch pulls amortise round trips: one poll can fetch many messages, which is both cheaper than one push per message and easier to bound.

Failure handling is uniform: a failed poll is a retried call rather than an event arriving while the application is in an undefined state, and a restarted consumer needs no re-registration - it resumes from its last acknowledgement.
Bounded batches cap the blast radius: the amount of unprocessed work a crash can lose or repeat is a configured number, not whatever the transport happened to send.
Batch jobs, admin tools and on-demand drains reuse the same consumer, because consuming is a call rather than a running listener.
tradeoffs: Latency versus cost: the idle interval sets the worst-case latency for a message that arrives just after a poll, so a short interval buys empty calls and CPU while a long one delays processing - a tension push delivery does not have.
An idle poll is never free: it is still a fetch or a round trip, and one polling thread per channel scales poorly compared with a demultiplexer.

Liveness coupling in brokered channels: the poll call is also the heartbeat, so a consumer that stops calling it (for example while processing a long batch) is evicted from its group and its partitions are rebalanced.

Acknowledgement windows must be chosen deliberately: acknowledging at fetch time loses in-flight messages on a crash, acknowledging after processing duplicates them, so at-least-once plus idempotent handlers is the usual price.
Backpressure is displaced onto the channel: a consumer that stops pulling lets the backlog grow until the channel expires or discards messages instead of slowing the producer.
Consumer objects are frequently not thread-safe and are bound to one session or partition assignment, so scaling out means competing consumers, which reintroduces ordering and affinity concerns.
More moving parts than a listener registration in the simple case: loop, idle policy, batch cap, shutdown signal, acknowledgement point and commit cadence must all be designed and monitored.

participants.responsibility: Endpoint object that exposes the pull to application code (receive/poll/receiveNoWait), translates it into the channel's retrieval API, owns the idle policy and returns at most a bounded batch.
Decides when to pull and how much it is ready to handle, processes each returned message, acknowledges it and owns the shutdown signal.
Holds messages until they are pulled; a queue, topic, mailbox, table or any other medium that exposes retrieval without push.
Application logic invoked once per pulled message; its successful completion defines the point at which acknowledgement is safe.
Transport-specific layer that implements one pull (a fetch, a timed receive, a table read) and the acknowledgement call; the only participant that knows the transport API.

use_cases: Consumers of pull-based brokers (Kafka and most message-queue APIs) where fetching is the only retrieval mechanism and each poll returns a bounded batch.
Batch jobs, nightly syncs and admin tools that drain a queue or a table on their own schedule and then stop, with no listener process to keep alive.
Integrations with systems that cannot push: a database table used as a queue, a watched directory, or a legacy device answered by a request/response API.
Workers that must not exceed a downstream capacity, where the poll rate itself is the throttle.
Single-threaded consumers with a poll affinity (one consumer per partition or session) that process batches and commit acknowledgement explicitly.
Constrained components where holding a long-lived push connection and a callback dispatch path costs more than a periodic fetch.

Apache Kafka consumers use KafkaConsumer.poll(Duration) to fetch records on demand, with max.poll.records bounding each returned batch and max.poll.interval.ms constraining processing time between polls.
Amazon SQS workers call ReceiveMessage with MaxNumberOfMessages and WaitTimeSeconds for bounded, optionally long-polled receives, then delete or extend visibility only after successful handling.
PostgreSQL-backed queue workers claim jobs with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED in short transactions, letting competing consumers pull unlocked rows without waiting on one another.
avoid_when: The channel can push and the consumer is always ready: an Event-Driven Consumer (listener, callback, subscription) reacts with lower latency and no idle polling cost.
Latency is the product requirement: a poll interval is a latency floor that tuning cannot remove, so prefer push delivery or server-side long polling where the protocol offers it.
The consumer must scale to very many channels: one polling thread or task per channel does not scale - use an I/O demultiplexer or an async runtime instead.
A framework or client already owns the loop (broker SDK poll loops, framework listeners): re-implementing it duplicates the idle and acknowledgement semantics that library already gets right.
The interaction is a direct request/response call: the call you already make is the pull, and wrapping it in a consumer object with a loop adds indirection without benefit.
anti_patterns: Hot-spin polling: a receiveNoWait/try_recv/poll(0) loop with no idle interval or backoff, burning CPU and hammering the channel to be told 'nothing yet'.
Rebuilding an event-driven consumer badly: polling a channel that can push, so the push path's latency advantage is paid for and then lost to the timer.
Acknowledging at fetch time (auto-commit, AUTO_ACKNOWLEDGE, task_done before the work) so a crash loses in-flight messages that no one notices until an audit.
Unbounded batches processed inside the polling loop until the broker evicts the consumer for missing its poll interval.
One shared poll loop across threads for a consumer object that is not thread-safe, producing duplicate delivery, offset corruption or both.
Treating the idle tick (empty batch, timeout return, Empty exception) as an error or as end-of-stream, so a quiet channel pages the on-call engineer or shuts the consumer down.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: the consumer owns retrieval, timing and acknowledgement; the handler owns processing and knows nothing about the transport.
Inversion of control by the caller: the application, not the transport, decides when work is accepted, so flow control is expressed as not calling.
Single responsibility per participant: one object pulls, one object processes, one adapter knows how to talk to the transport.
Explicit contracts over incidental timing: idle interval, batch bound, acknowledgement point and shutdown path are configured decisions, not side effects.
Design for at-least-once: make the handler idempotent rather than assuming the acknowledgement window can be closed exactly once.
Dependency inversion: the consumer depends on a pull interface (receive/poll/ack), so the transport can be replaced by a fake in tests.
best_practices: Bound the batch (max.poll.records, a fetch limit, a maxsize queue) and keep each iteration short enough to keep polling on schedule for the transport's session or visibility timeout.
Make the idle policy explicit: a timeout on every receive, a fixed or exponential backoff with a ceiling when nothing arrives, and no zero-timeout spins.
Acknowledge only after processing succeeds - commit offsets, complete the message, call task_done in a finally - and make the handler idempotent, because redelivery is then possible.
Provide a shutdown path that unblocks the consumer: close/CompleteAdding, a cancellation token or signal, wakeup(), or a cooperative stop flag checked by the receive predicate.
Confine a consumer to one thread or coroutine and scale with competing consumers, each with its own session or partition assignment; never share a consumer object across threads.
Instrument the loop - idle polls, batch sizes, processed counts, commit latency and channel lag - because the pull rate is the parameter an operator will tune.
Prefer the transport's timed/long-poll hooks (maxWaitTime, receive(timeout), long polling) over a tight sleep-poll: the server can wait more cheaply than the client can spin.
sources: Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Messaging, and Deploying Messaging Solutions, Addison-Wesley (2003) - Chapter 10, Messaging Endpoints: Polling Consumer.
